The core contribution of BAP lies in its ability to identify and exploit parallelizable branches within DNN models, particularly those commonly found in Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and transformer-based architectures. The authors propose a runtime model analysis pipeline that automatically locates these parallel branches, enabling concurrent execution through a multithreading approach. This is achieved through a branch-aware memory allocation strategy, which isolates memory management at the granularity of layers and branches, minimizing data conflicts and optimizing memory reuse. The multithreading implementation leverages the identified parallel branches to accelerate inference on mobile CPUs. The authors evaluated BAP on a diverse set of devices, including Raspberry Pi 4B, Pixel 6, Google Pixel 4a, P30 Pro, and various mobile phones, demonstrating significant improvements in latency, memory efficiency, and energy consumption compared to a naive TFLite implementation. Specifically, the paper reports up to 38.5% reduction in inference latency, 15.6x memory savings, and 20.2% energy cost reduction across various mobile platforms. The methodology involves a graph analysis and branch identification algorithm that operates on the computational graph of the DNN model, identifying parallelizable branches based on the presence of multiple independent operations within a single layer. These branches are then executed in parallel using multithreading, with a branch-aware memory allocation strategy that isolates memory management for each branch. The paper's significance lies in its practical approach to optimizing DNN inference on mobile devices, addressing the growing demand for efficient on-device machine learning. By focusing on parallelizable branches and employing a branch-aware memory allocation strategy, BAP offers a promising solution for improving the performance of DNNs on resource-constrained hardware.
